"The Fiedler vector is the last non-uniform heat left." . . . Today we make that picture precise: 1. Graph matrices **are** $-\operatorname{div}\nabla$ (for the right measures). 2. The random walk and the heat kernel; measures vs. functions; the spectral gap. Next lecture: how fast the walk converges — distances to $\pi$, mixing time, and bounds on the spectral gap. ::: notes ~3 min. Conventions as in Lecture 1: P = D^{-1}A row-stochastic, distributions are row vectors on the left, functions are column vectors on the right. ::: # §1 · Graphs as differential operators {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## The gradient {.scrollable} - $G=(V,E,w)$ __undirected, connected__, weighted graph with $w_{ij}>0$. - $\mathbb{R}^V$: the space of real functions on vertices, e.g., potentials such as temperature. - Orient each edge arbitrarily, $e=(i\to j)$ and define the _discrete gradient_ operator as: $$ \nabla : \mathbb R^V \to \mathbb R^E, \qquad (\nabla f)(e) = f(j) - f(i). $$ As a matrix: the signed incidence matrix $B \in \mathbb R^{E\times V}$. . . . - A function on vertices $\mapsto$ a flow on edges. - $\ker\nabla$ = constants (connected graph) — "$\nabla f = 0 \Rightarrow f$ constant." . . . ::: notes Thinking of the graph as a discrete manifold $M$, this is analogous to the tangent bundle $TM$ of $M$. Functions in $\mathbb{R}^E$ are analogous to vector fields on $M$. Combinatorially, they can also be interpreted as flows along edges. ::: ## Example: $f$ and $\nabla f$ on a graph ::: {#30c340a0 .cell fig-height='3.8' fig-width='11' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Blue = $f$ at each vertex; orange = $(\nabla f)(e) = f(j)-f(i)$ on each oriented edge. Each row of $B$ is $-1$ at the tail, $+1$ at the head: $(Bf)_e = (\nabla f)(e)$.](lecture2_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){width=938 height=347} ::: ::: . . . ::: {.box .small} The flow $\nabla f \in \mathbb{R}^E$ can be thought of as a vector field, i.e., a member of the tangent bundle, where $(\nabla f)_e$ represents the directional derivative of the function $f$ along edge $e$. ::: ## Divergence $= -\nabla^*$, and the measure matters {.smaller} ::: box In continuous space (e.g., on a smooth compact manifold $M$ with no boundary), the adjoint of the gradient with respect to the standard $L^2$ inner product is the negative divergence: $$ \int_M f\,(-\operatorname{div} X) \, dV = \int_M \langle \nabla f, X\rangle \, dV $$ ::: To make this work on graphs, we need to define appropriate inner products on both the space of functions on vertices and the space of flows on edges. | | manifold | graph | |---|---|---| | on vector fields | metric $g$ | edge weights: $\langle X,Y\rangle_w = \sum_e w_e X_eY_e$ | | on functions | volume $dV$ | vertex measure $m$: $\langle f,g\rangle_m = \sum_i m_if_ig_i$ | . . . Define $\nabla^*_m$ by $\langle\nabla f, X\rangle_w = \langle f,\nabla_m^*X\rangle_m$. Expanding, for coordinate $i$: $$ (\nabla_m^* X)_i = \frac{1}{m_i}\Big(\sum_{e \text{ into } i} w_eX_e - \sum_{e \text{ out of } i} w_eX_e\Big) =: -(\operatorname{div}_m X)_i . $$ Divergence = net weighted **outflow per unit vertex mass**. ## Example: the divergence of $\nabla f$ ::: {#33f4cdc1 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='6' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Green = $\operatorname{div}(\nabla f)_i$ (counting measure, $m\equiv1$, unweighted): outflow minus inflow at $i$. E.g. at $D$: $(-3.5) - \big((-1.5)+(2.5)\big) = -4.5$.](lecture2_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=523 height=327} ::: ::: . . . ::: {.box .small} Like in continuous space, $-\nabla^*$ measures the net outflow of a vector field per unit volume (or vertex mass, in the graph case). ::: ::: notes Same graph and same flow X = grad f as two slides ago (orange edge labels unchanged). Now sum signed flow at each vertex: div(X)_i = sum of X_e over edges leaving i, minus sum of X_e over edges entering i. Check: the five div values sum to 0 (telescoping — every edge contributes +X_e to one endpoint and -X_e to the other). Also: div(grad f) = -Lf here, matching div = -nabla^* and L = nabla^* nabla for the counting measure, previewed on the next slide. ::: ## Both Laplacians are $-\operatorname{div}\nabla$ {.smaller} ::: box **Proposition.** $\displaystyle(\nabla_m^*\nabla f)_i = \frac1{m_i}\sum_{j\sim i}w_{ij}(f_i - f_j)$. Hence - $m \equiv \mathbf 1$ (counting measure): $\;\nabla^*\nabla = B^\top WB = D - A = L$, the **combinatorial Laplacian**; - $m = d$ (degree measure): $\;\nabla_d^*\nabla = D^{-1}L = L_{rw}$, the **random-walk Laplacian**. ::: . . . - Self-adjoint and PSD in $L^2(m)$ **for every $m$** — nothing to check. - The **normalized Laplacian** $\mathcal L = D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}$ is $L_{rw}$ moved to the unweighted space by the isometry $f\mapsto D^{1/2}f$. . . . > Lecture 1: "a change of which inner product, not a repair of a broken operator." Now with a reason: **the vertex measure is the volume form.** ::: notes Proof: each edge between i and a neighbor j contributes w_ij (f_i - f_j) regardless of orientation (two cases: e into i or out of i). ::: ## Green's identity and the Dirichlet form {.smaller} By construction ("integration by parts"): $$ \langle f,\nabla_m^*\nabla g\rangle_m = \langle\nabla f,\nabla g\rangle_w = \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}\,(f_i - f_j)(g_i - g_j) $$ $$ \longleftrightarrow\qquad \int f\,(-\Delta g) = \int\langle\nabla f,\nabla g\rangle . $$ - **No boundary term**: graph Laplacians have Neumann boundary conditions built in. . . . With $m = \mathbf 1$ (counting measure), we get the __energy__: $$\langle f,\nabla_m^*\nabla f\rangle_m = \langle\nabla f,\nabla f\rangle_w = \sum w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2 \leftrightarrow \int|\nabla f|^2$$ . . . With $m = \pi$, $\pi_i = d_i/\mathrm{vol}(V)$, the normalized degree distribution, we get the **Dirichlet form**: $$ \mathcal E(f,g) := \langle f, L_{rw}g\rangle_\pi = \frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)(g_i-g_j). $$ ## Dictionary {.smaller} | Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ | weighted graph $G = (V,E,w)$ | |---|---| | metric $g$ (conductivity) | edge weights $w$ | | volume measure $dV$ | vertex measure $m$ (counting, or degree) | | $\operatorname{div} = -\nabla^*$ | $\operatorname{div}_m = -\nabla_m^*$ | | $\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\nabla \succeq 0$ | $L$ ($m=\mathbf 1$), $\;L_{rw}$ ($m = d$) | | $\int_M|\nabla f|^2\,dV$ | $\sum_{ij}w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2$ | | Neumann boundary conditions | automatic | | weighted manifold $(M,g,e^{-U}dV)$: $\;\Delta_U = -e^{U}\operatorname{div}(e^{-U}\nabla\,\cdot)$ | $L_{rw}$, self-adjoint in $L^2(\pi)$ | | Poincaré: $\operatorname{Var}(f)\le C\int|\nabla f|^2$ | $\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)\le\lambda^{-1}\mathcal E(f,f)$ (soon) | ::: box __For later__:Weighted-manifold row: $\Delta_U$ is (minus) the generator of **Langevin diffusion** with stationary density $\propto e^{-U}$. $L_{rw}$ is its discrete twin, with $\pi\propto d$ playing $e^{-U}$. ::: ## Sanity check: finite differences - **Path**, weights $h^{-2}$: $\;(Lf)_i = h^{-2}(2f_i - f_{i-1} - f_{i+1})\to -f''$ — the **3-point stencil**. - **Grid**, weights $h^{-2}$: $\;(Lf)_{i,j} = h^{-2}(4f_{i,j} - f_{i\pm1,j} - f_{i,j\pm1})\to-\Delta f$ — the **5-point stencil**. ::: {#e14f7122 .cell fig-height='4.6' fig-width='11' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lecture2_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=985 height=424} ::: ::: ::: notes Interior grid vertex: degree 4, so L is exactly the 5-point stencil for −Δ. Boundary vertex (green): degree 3; L drops the missing term, equivalent to a ghost value equal to the vertex's own value, i.e. zero normal derivative (Neumann). Dirichlet would keep the diagonal at 4/h² and lose 1 from the kernel. The cycle's spectrum (sampled Fourier modes) is computed in Lecture 3, §4. ::: ## Recap: properties of the Laplacian {.smaller} Both $L$ and $L_{rw}$ — any $\nabla_m^*\nabla$ — share three structural facts, for free: ::: box **1. Self-adjoint** in $L^2(m)$, for *every* $m$: $L = \nabla_m^*\nabla$ has the form $A^*A$. ::: . . . ::: box **2. Positive semi-definite.** $\langle f,Lf\rangle_m = \langle\nabla f,\nabla f\rangle_w = \sum_{ij}w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2\ge0$. ::: . . . ::: box **3. Spectrum is bounded.** $G$ connected $\Rightarrow$ $0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$, with $\ker L = \operatorname{span}(\mathbf 1)$ ($\lambda_1$ simple). Upper end: $\lambda_n(L)\le 2d_{\max}$ (Gershgorin); for $L_{rw}$ and $\mathcal L$ ($m=d$), which are similar to each other: $\lambda_n\le 2$. ::: . . . > Self-adjoint + PSD + bounded spectrum $\Rightarrow$ an orthonormal eigenbasis and a well-behaved heat kernel $H_t = e^{-tL_{rw}}$ — exactly what the rest of this lecture, and the next, leans on. ::: notes (1)-(2) are immediate from the A*A form shown on the "Both Laplacians" slide — nothing new to check for any m or any edge weights. (3): kernel = constants because G is connected (gradient slide, §1). Gershgorin for the upper bound: row i of L has diagonal d_i and off-diagonal entries summing to d_i in absolute value, so every eigenvalue lies in some disc [0, 2d_i], hence lambda_n <= 2 d_max. For L_rw = D^{-1}L (similar to the symmetric L = D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2}), the same argument with row sums of L_rw equal to 1 gives lambda_n <= 2 directly — this is the bound quoted later (spectral decomposition slide, §2). This slide is pure bookkeeping — the content is all already on screen earlier, just gathered in one place before we start using it. ::: # §2 · The random walk and measure/function duality {background-color="#1c1b19"} ## The random walk transition matrix ::: box At each step, the random walk picks a neighbor with probability proportional to the edge weight. The __probability transition matrix__ is: $$P = D^{-1}A, \quad P_{ij} = \Pr[X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t = i] = w_{ij}/d_i.$$ ::: . . . __Stationary distribution__ is $\pi_i = d_i/\mathrm{vol}(V)$: $$\pi^\top P = \pi^\top D^{-1}A = \frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\mathbf 1^\top A = \frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(V)}\mathbf 1^\top D = \pi^\top.$$ ## One matrix, two actions :::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Measures** (row vectors) $$\mu^\top\ \mapsto\ \mu^\top P$$ law of $X_1$ when $X_0\sim\mu$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Functions** (column vectors) $$(Pf)(i) = \mathbb E[f(X_1)\mid X_0 = i]$$ local **averaging** ::: :::::: . . . Canoical pairing $\langle\mu,f\rangle = \mu^\top f = \mathbb E_\mu f$: $$ \langle\mu^\top P, f\rangle = \mu^\top Pf = \langle\mu, Pf\rangle . $$ Evolve the distribution forward and observe, **or** evolve the observable and average against the start. Same number. ## Continuous time: heat kernel Jump at the rings of a rate-1 Poisson clock: $$ H_t = \sum_{k\ge0}e^{-t}\frac{t^k}{k!}P^k = e^{-t(I-P)} = e^{-tL_{rw}},\qquad (H_tf)(i) = \mathbb E_i f(X_t). $$ . . . - **Backward** (functions): $\partial_tf_t = -L_{rw}f_t$ — Lecture 1's heat equation. - **Forward** (measures): $\mu_t^\top = \mu_0^\top H_t$, $\;\partial_t\mu_t^\top = -\mu_t^\top L_{rw}$ — master / Fokker–Planck. ## Semigroups and generators We will see that the heat kernel is the special case of a **semigroup**: __Definition (Semigroup):__ A family of operators $\{H_t\}_{t\ge0}$ is a semigroup if: - $H_0 = I$, and - $H_{s+t} = H_s H_t$ for all $s,t\ge0$. **Generator** (Markov convention): The generator $\mathcal{A}$ describes the infinitesimal evolution of the semigroup: $$\mathcal A = \frac{d}{dt}H_t\big|_{t=0} = P - I = -L_{rw}$$ ::: notes Sign: we keep the positive operator L_rw ⪰ 0 to match Δ = −div∇ ⪰ 0 from Lecture 1; Markov literature calls A = −L_rw the generator. Semigroup properties used later: H_0 = I, H_{s+t} = H_s H_t, H_t 1 = 1, positivity. Everything below uses only these + self-adjointness, which is why it transfers to diffusions. ::: ## Advantages of Continuous Time - Can differentiate by time: $\partial_t H_t = -L_{rw} H_t$. - Avoids the bipartite problem: eigenvalues of $H_t$ are in $(0,1]$ rather than $P$ having $-1$. Cycle ($n$ even), grid, binary tree: all **bipartite** $\Rightarrow$ $P$ has eigenvalue $-1$. The discrete walk from a vertex **never converges** — it alternates sides. . . . This problem can alternatively be fixed by making the walk **lazy**: $$P_{\rm lazy} = \tfrac12(I + P) = I - \tfrac12L_{rw}$$, This has eigenvalues $1 - \tfrac{\lambda_k}{2}\in[0,1]$. We work in continuous time; discrete-time statements follow with $e^{-\lambda}\to 1-\lambda/2$. ## Stationarity and detailed balance __Question__: What does self-adjointness in $L^2(\pi)$ imply for the behavior of the random walk? . . . . . . **Detailed balance:** $$ \pi_iP_{ij} = \frac{w_{ij}}{\mathrm{vol}(V)} = \pi_jP_{ji}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\Pi P = P^\top\Pi,\quad\Pi = \operatorname{diag}(\pi). $$ . . . $\Longleftrightarrow$ $P$, $L_{rw}$, $H_t$ are **self-adjoint in** $L^2(\pi)$: $$ \langle f, Pg\rangle_\pi = f^\top\Pi Pg = f^\top P^\top\Pi g = \langle Pf, g\rangle_\pi . $$ Same fact as $\nabla_\pi^*\nabla = \mathrm{vol}(V)\,L_{rw}$, now seen probabilistically. ## Densities are functions {.smaller} Write $\mu = \Pi h$, i.e. $h = d\mu/d\pi$, $\;h_i = \mu_i/\pi_i$. ::: box **Proposition.** If $\mu_t^\top = \mu_0^\top H_t$ then $h_t = H_t^*h_0$, with $H_t^* = \Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi$ the adjoint in $L^2(\pi)$. For reversible walks $H_t^* = H_t$: $$h_t = H_th_0 .$$ **Densities obey the same heat equation as observables.** ::: . . . *Proof.* $h_t = \Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi h_0$, and $\langle f,\Pi^{-1}H_t^\top\Pi g\rangle_\pi = f^\top H_t^\top\Pi g = \langle H_tf,g\rangle_\pi$. Detailed balance: $\Pi H_t = H_t^\top\Pi$. $\square$ . . . - $\mu\mapsto\mu/\pi$ is an **isometry** from $(\mathbb R^V,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/\pi})$ (measures) to $L^2(\pi)$ (functions): the Riesz map. - Non-reversible chains: $h_t$ evolves by the **time-reversed** semigroup. We'll meet this again with general Markov semigroups. ## Demo: measures vs densities — split and aggregate {.smaller} open in new tab ↗ ::: notes One loop: vertex mass --D⁻¹--> value on each edge-end --send--> far end --A--> vertex mass. Measures and densities are the same loop cut at different places. Measures (start at red vertex mass): split (D⁻¹), send, aggregate (A): μᵀ ↦ μᵀD⁻¹A = μᵀP. Mass is conserved. Densities (start at blue value, x = D⁻¹μ = h/vol): send copies, aggregate (A), average (D⁻¹): x ↦ D⁻¹Ax = Px. Constants are preserved. Point out: in density mode the red intermediate Ax_t is exactly μ_{t+1}; the invariant μ_t = D x_t holds at every step. Run it: μ_t → π ∝ degree (uneven red bars), x_t → constant 1/vol (flat blue bars). This makes the previous two slides concrete: π is the fixed point of the measure loop, and densities evolve by the same P as functions (they converge to constants). Graph and starting values are from the old SGT figure (degrees 1,3,2,2; vol = 8). It has a triangle, so the discrete walk is aperiodic and converges. ::: ## Spectral decomposition and the Poincaré inequality {.smaller} $L_{rw}$ self-adjoint in $L^2(\pi)$ $\Rightarrow$ orthonormal eigenbasis $\varphi_1 = \mathbf 1,\varphi_2,\dots,\varphi_n$, $\;0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\le\dots\le\lambda_n\le2$: $$ H_tf = \sum_ke^{-\lambda_kt}\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi\varphi_k,\qquad \mathcal E(f,f) = \sum_k\lambda_k\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi^2, $$ $$ \operatorname{Var}_\pi(f) = \sum_{k\ge2}\langle f,\varphi_k\rangle_\pi^2 . $$ . . . **Spectral gap** $\lambda := \lambda_2(L_{rw})$. Courant–Fischer: $$ \lambda = \min_{f\ \text{non-const}}\frac{\mathcal E(f,f)}{\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{\ \lambda\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f)\le\mathcal E(f,f)\ } $$ **Poincaré inequality**: "small gradient $\Rightarrow$ nearly constant." **Relaxation time** $t_{\rm rel} := 1/\lambda$. . . . ::: box **The variance is an energy too.** $\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f) = \sum_{a
